identity.title: Skip a Layer or Loop It? Learning Program-of-Layers in LLMs

problem.claim: LLMs ordinarily infer with a fixed-depth, fixed-order pass through all layers, motivating input-specific execution programs.

gap.claim: Fixed-depth execution may capture only a narrow subset of an LLM’s latent reasoning capacity.

contributions.claim: The authors report broadly occurring, training-free program-of-layers execution that packs pretrained layers into modules and skips or loops them per input.
They propose a lightweight predictor that generates input-specific programs to skip or repeat pretrained layers.
They report improved accuracy, often with fewer executed layers, relative to standard inference and prior dynamic-depth methods, including under out-of-distribution evaluation.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their approach through flexible, dynamic programs that can both skip and loop pretrained layers for each input, without training the base layers.

author_reported_evidence.claim: For most inputs, substantially shorter executions reportedly achieve the same or better accuracy; alternative programs can reportedly correct some original LLM errors while using fewer layers.

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the authors report consistent accuracy gains over standard inference and prior dynamic-depth methods, often with fewer executed layers, and persistence of gains under out-of-distribution evaluation.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs are described as using fixed-depth, fixed-order, non-recurrent execution.
The authors report flexible, training-free programs that skip or loop pretrained layer modules per input.
Shorter alternative programs may preserve or improve accuracy and correct some baseline errors, suggesting multiple valid latent computations.
A lightweight program predictor is proposed and evaluated on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with reported gains over standard and prior dynamic-depth inference, including out of distribution.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a flexible execution mechanism with evidence about both accuracy and computation length, including error correction by alternative programs.

lessons.interpretation: A method claim becomes more informative when it specifies the adaptive action and measures its quality–cost tradeoff.
lessons.application: When presenting adaptive inference, report both task performance and execution cost, and test whether alternative execution paths repair baseline errors.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when computation cost is fixed by the deployment setting or when no meaningful alternative execution paths exist.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify benchmark names, model families, layer-count reductions, or numerical accuracy changes.
It does not define how PoLar programs are generated or trained, nor the scope of “wide existence” and “most inputs.”
Details of the out-of-distribution splits and comparisons with prior dynamic-depth methods are unspecified.
